newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Oil firms want Hong Kong trade policies unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Oil firms want Hong Kong trade policies unchanged.

text.p: Asian oil companies hope oil trade policies in Hong Kong will stay unchanged after its handover to China on July 1, traders said on Thursday.
"We hope that the status quo will remain as long as possible," said a trader at a European oil company in Hong Kong.
Other traders said they wanted the Basic Law, the mini-constitution that guarantees the Special Administrative Region a high degree of autonomy for 50 years, to be extended beyond that period.

"Hong Kong forms part of a vital trade route for oil exports from the rest of Asia to China. It would be good if trade policies remain the way they are because they work for both buyers and sellers," said a trader in Singapore.
While most traders do not see immediate policy changes to the oil trade in Hong Kong after the handover, uncertainties abound over its longer-term outlook.
"Hong Kong will be governed by China and is no longer under British rule; there will be some changes in the future," said a source at state-owned Chinese Resources Company (CRC) in Hong Kong.
But others were more optimistic, citing the rapid growth in oil exports that would ride the burgeoning development in China's special economic zones.
"Growth of our business in Hong Kong will really mirror that of the southern China market," said George Good, managing director of Mobil Oil Hong Kong.
"We would look for double digit growth for southern China which is the market we would serve out of Hong Kong," he added.
Mobil operates a one million-barrel storage facility in Hong Kong which serves its oil markets and those of southern China.
"Hong Kong is likely to remain as it is but interaction between China and Hong Kong may change in the foreseeable future," the trader in Singapore said.

Hong Kong currently gives a preferential custom import tax of six percent, compared to the normal rate of 11 percent, for diesel imports to selected countries. These include Singapore, Japan and South Korea.
But traders do not have to pay any import tax for bonded oil products sold to Hong Kong which are re-exported to China.
At present the consumption tax for diesel, which forms the bulk of oil product imports to China from Hong Kong, is valued at 10 cents per litre and has a value-added tax of 17 percent.
Hong Kong exports about 200,000 tonnes of oil products to China each month, most of which is diesel.
